# Sources RAG entry point

Answer only from the assigned MCP dataset.

The dataset contains source records (with `path` `sources`): original evidence from documents, messages, meetings, and task systems. Use these records to answer and cite.

## Retrieval

The `mcp__tl-v1__ragflow_retrieval` tool is deferred. Load it first with ToolSearch using the query `select:mcp__tl-v1__ragflow_retrieval`.

On every retrieval, pass only the dataset ID assigned to this arm and use `metadata_condition` to restrict `path` to `sources`. Use concrete identifiers and topic terms from the question, and retrieve further evidence as needed to answer all material parts.

Pass these values on every `ragflow_retrieval` call, and do not vary them between calls:

```
page_size: 10
vector_similarity_weight: 0.3
similarity_threshold: 0.2
top_k: 1024
keyword: false
```

If the retrieved sources do not support an answer, say so. Cite the source records used for the answer.

Return the complete answer in the final response. Your final response IS the deliverable — it must contain the full answer text verbatim, not a summary or a pointer to work done.

---

Beyond Docker and Windows packaging, which compliance and audit items still hold v1.0.0 as of **2026-09-22**? For each, give current status, the concrete defect or risk, and whether engineering search alone can close it.

Use only `tl-v1` MCP with `d13efb7c8a9a11f197db2303d7337e37` dataset to answer. Do not use web, local files, memory, or any other MCP dataset.

Use when: customize plugin, set up plugin, configure plugin, tailor plugin, adjust plugin settings, customize plugin connectors, customize plugin skill, tweak plugin, modify plugin configuration.
- cowork-plugin-management:create-cowork-plugin: Guide users through creating a new plugin from scratch in a cowork session. Use when users want to create a plugin, build a plugin, make a new plugin, develop a plugin, scaffold a plugin, start a plugin from scratch, or design a plugin. This skill requires Cowork mode with access to the outputs directory for delivering the final .plugin file.
- anthropic-skills:consolidate-memory: Reflective pass over your memory files — merge duplicates, fix stale facts, prune the index.
- anthropic-skills:doc-coauthoring: Guide users through a structured workflow for co-authoring documentation. Use when user wants to write documentation, proposals, technical specs, decision docs, or similar structured content. This workflow helps users efficiently transfer context, refine content through iteration, and verify the doc works for readers. Trigger when user mentions writing docs, creating proposals, drafting specs, or similar documentation tasks.
- anthropic-skills:docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx files) or Word templates (.dotx files). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, performing find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file, use this skill. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or general coding tasks unrelated to document generation.
- anthropic-skills:morning: Render the user's morning brief as a styled HTML artifact, or set it up as a recurring weekday task. Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead.
- anthropic-skills:pdf: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill.
- anthropic-skills:pptx: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email or summary); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user mentions "deck," "slides," "presentation," or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. If a .pptx or .potx file needs to be opened, created, or touched, use this skill.
- anthropic-skills:schedule: Create or update a scheduled task that runs automatically. Use when the user says things like "every day", "each morning", "remind me in an hour", "run this at noon", or wants to reschedule an existing task.
- anthropic-skills:setup-cowork: Guided Cowork setup — install role-matched plugins, connect your tools, try a skill.
- anthropic-skills:skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- anthropic-skills:xlsx: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

Security sign-off on the AES-256 at-rest pipeline was withheld until the fail-closed deletion behavior for interrupted redaction runs (T015) was confirmed Completed — an unencrypted partial output left on disk after a crash would have undermined the encryption guarantee entirely. **Owner**: Diana

**Document Key**: DOC-2035

**Last Updated**: 2026-08-07

## What Was Reviewed

- AES-256-GCM authenticated encryption applied to every redacted output file before it is written to its final location.

- Key handling confined to process memory; no plaintext key material written to disk or logs.

- Confirmed the pipeline degrades safely (refuses to write plaintext) if key material is unavailable, consistent with the fail-closed contract from T015.

**Source ID**: SRC-GDOC-35

# Crypto Sign-off: AES-256 At-Rest Encryption Pipeline

**Owner**: Diana

**Document Key**: DOC-2035

**Last Updated**: 2026-08-07

On machines without a hardware TPM, the volume key is still derived from a user passphrase via PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 at 100k iterations. This is not a blocker for the AES-256 pipeline sign-off itself, but Diana flagged it as a hardening follow-up: moving to Argon2id would meaningfully raise the cost of offline brute-force against weak passphrases on non-TPM hardware.

*Status*: AES-256 at-rest pipeline signed off as Completed. Passphrase-derived key hardening (Argon2id) tracked separately as a pre-v1.0 hardening item, not a sign-off condition.

**Owner**: Evan

**Document Key**: DOC-2039

**Last Updated**: 2026-09-02

## Current Blocker: Missing Code-Signing Certificate

The produced build artifact is unsigned, which triggers a SmartScreen warning and Defender flagging the binary as untrusted.

- **Impact**: Site IT policies commonly block execution of unsigned/SmartScreen-flagged binaries outright, which would prevent installation on target deployment workstations without a manual security-policy override.

- **Root Cause**: No code-signing certificate has been procured or configured in the Windows build pipeline yet.

**Source ID**: SRC-GDOC-39

# Privacy Design Note: Telemetry Opt-Out Flag Semantics

**Owner**: Diana

**Document Key**: DOC-2051

**Last Updated**: 2026-09-06

## Opt-Out Behaviour Designed

The CLI and API collect anonymous usage metrics (pages processed, OCR fallback rate) to help tune the detection engine. Setting `CIPHER_TELEMETRY=0`, or the equivalent GUI toggle, is designed to immediately stop all outbound telemetry traffic to the metrics endpoint.

**Source ID**: SRC-GDOC-51

# Privacy Design Note: Telemetry Opt-Out Flag Semantics

**Owner**: Diana

**Document Key**: DOC-2051

**Last Updated**: 2026-09-06

## Design-Time Issue Found and Patched: Pending-Queue Leak

While designing the flag semantics, testing surfaced that the opt-out flag blocked network egress correctly, but the `TelemetryLogger` kept writing event payloads to a local SQLite queue regardless. That meant re-enabling telemetry later would flush the entire backlog accumulated during the opt-out period, including events the user believed were never being recorded. The logger was patched to a no-op backend when opted out, closing that gap before the flag semantics were finalized.

**Source ID**: SRC-GDOC-51

# Privacy Design Note: Telemetry Opt-Out Flag Semantics

**Owner**: Diana

**Document Key**: DOC-2051

**Last Updated**: 2026-09-06

## Verification (Retrospective)

A network trace on 2026-08-24 confirmed zero outbound telemetry traffic once the opt-out flag is set, closing the CLI-side verification as Completed.

**Source ID**: SRC-GDOC-51

# Privacy Design Note: Telemetry Opt-Out Flag Semantics

**Owner**: Diana

**Document Key**: DOC-2051

**Last Updated**: 2026-09-06

## Remaining Limitation

The third-party Electron crash reporter (Sentry) has not been audited for whether it independently respects the opt-out environment variable or requires its own disable hook for minidump uploads.

*Note*: CLI-side telemetry opt-out is verified. Full privacy compliance for air-gapped/opt-out users cannot be claimed until the Sentry crash-reporter path is audited separately.

# Privacy Design Note: Telemetry Opt-Out Flag Semantics

**Owner**: Diana

**Document Key**: DOC-2051

**Last Updated**: 2026-09-06

## Opt-Out Behaviour Designed

The CLI and API collect anonymous usage metrics (pages processed, OCR fallback rate) to help tune the detection engine. Setting `CIPHER_TELEMETRY=0`, or the equivalent GUI toggle, is designed to immediately stop all outbound telemetry traffic to the metrics endpoint.

**Source ID**: SRC-GDOC-51

# Privacy Design Note: Telemetry Opt-Out Flag Semantics

**Owner**: Diana

**Document Key**: DOC-2051

**Last Updated**: 2026-09-06

## Design-Time Issue Found and Patched: Pending-Queue Leak

While designing the flag semantics, testing surfaced that the opt-out flag blocked network egress correctly, but the `TelemetryLogger` kept writing event payloads to a local SQLite queue regardless. That meant re-enabling telemetry later would flush the entire backlog accumulated during the opt-out period, including events the user believed were never being recorded. The logger was patched to a no-op backend when opted out, closing that gap before the flag semantics were finalized.

**Source ID**: SRC-GDOC-51

# Privacy Design Note: Telemetry Opt-Out Flag Semantics

**Owner**: Diana

**Document Key**: DOC-2051

**Last Updated**: 2026-09-06

## Verification (Retrospective)

A network trace on 2026-08-24 confirmed zero outbound telemetry traffic once the opt-out flag is set, closing the CLI-side verification as Completed.

**Source ID**: SRC-GDOC-51

# Privacy Design Note: Telemetry Opt-Out Flag Semantics

**Owner**: Diana

**Document Key**: DOC-2051

**Last Updated**: 2026-09-06

## Remaining Limitation

The third-party Electron crash reporter (Sentry) has not been audited for whether it independently respects the opt-out environment variable or requires its own disable hook for minidump uploads.

*Note*: CLI-side telemetry opt-out is verified. Full privacy compliance for air-gapped/opt-out users cannot be claimed until the Sentry crash-reporter path is audited separately.

# Design Note: Reproducible Offline Test Harness

**Owner**: Diana

**Document Key**: DOC-2046

**Last Updated**: 2026-08-06

## Why a Harness, Not a One-Off VM

An earlier air-gapped check (see the manual single-VM USB-transfer test) proved the CLI *can* run offline, but it wasn't repeatable — every run required hand-configuring a disconnected machine. T027 calls for a harness that reliably and automatically denies network access on every run, so the offline claim can be re-verified continuously rather than checked once by hand.

**Source ID**: SRC-GDOC-46

# Design Note: Reproducible Offline Test Harness

**Owner**: Diana

**Document Key**: DOC-2046

**Last Updated**: 2026-08-06

## Harness Design

- Runs the batch CLI inside a dedicated Linux network namespace (`ip netns`) with no interfaces attached except loopback, rather than relying on a physically air-gapped machine.

- A wrapper script asserts the namespace has zero routable interfaces before invoking the CLI, and fails the harness run outright — rather than silently proceeding — if any route to the outside world is detected.

- Harness output is a pass/fail plus a captured syscall-level network-attempt log, so any code path that *tries* to reach the network, even if it degrades gracefully, is visible for follow-up.

**Source ID**: SRC-GDOC-46

# Design Note: Reproducible Offline Test Harness

**Owner**: Diana

**Document Key**: DOC-2046

**Last Updated**: 2026-08-06

## Status

Denies network access reliably and repeatably across local test runs. The harness is not yet wired into CI (it currently runs manually), and it validates network denial only — it does not itself certify the full offline batch run for compliance purposes; that sign-off is a separate step.

*Status*: Active. Harness reliably enforces network denial; CI integration and any compliance certification are separate, not-yet-complete steps.

# Design Note: Reproducible Offline Test Harness

**Owner**: Diana

**Document Key**: DOC-2046

**Last Updated**: 2026-08-06

## Why a Harness, Not a One-Off VM

An earlier air-gapped check (see the manual single-VM USB-transfer test) proved the CLI *can* run offline, but it wasn't repeatable — every run required hand-configuring a disconnected machine. T027 calls for a harness that reliably and automatically denies network access on every run, so the offline claim can be re-verified continuously rather than checked once by hand.

**Source ID**: SRC-GDOC-46

# Design Note: Reproducible Offline Test Harness

**Owner**: Diana

**Document Key**: DOC-2046

**Last Updated**: 2026-08-06

## Harness Design

- Runs the batch CLI inside a dedicated Linux network namespace (`ip netns`) with no interfaces attached except loopback, rather than relying on a physically air-gapped machine.

- A wrapper script asserts the namespace has zero routable interfaces before invoking the CLI, and fails the harness run outright — rather than silently proceeding — if any route to the outside world is detected.

- Harness output is a pass/fail plus a captured syscall-level network-attempt log, so any code path that *tries* to reach the network, even if it degrades gracefully, is visible for follow-up.

**Source ID**: SRC-GDOC-46

# Privacy Design Note: Telemetry Opt-Out Flag Semantics

**Owner**: Diana

**Document Key**: DOC-2051

**Last Updated**: 2026-09-06

## Opt-Out Behaviour Designed

The CLI and API collect anonymous usage metrics (pages processed, OCR fallback rate) to help tune the detection engine. Setting `CIPHER_TELEMETRY=0`, or the equivalent GUI toggle, is designed to immediately stop all outbound telemetry traffic to the metrics endpoint.

**Source ID**: SRC-GDOC-51

# Privacy Design Note: Telemetry Opt-Out Flag Semantics

**Owner**: Diana

**Document Key**: DOC-2051

**Last Updated**: 2026-09-06

## Design-Time Issue Found and Patched: Pending-Queue Leak

While designing the flag semantics, testing surfaced that the opt-out flag blocked network egress correctly, but the `TelemetryLogger` kept writing event payloads to a local SQLite queue regardless. That meant re-enabling telemetry later would flush the entire backlog accumulated during the opt-out period, including events the user believed were never being recorded. The logger was patched to a no-op backend when opted out, closing that gap before the flag semantics were finalized.

**Source ID**: SRC-GDOC-51

# Privacy Design Note: Telemetry Opt-Out Flag Semantics

**Owner**: Diana

**Document Key**: DOC-2051

**Last Updated**: 2026-09-06

## Verification (Retrospective)

A network trace on 2026-08-24 confirmed zero outbound telemetry traffic once the opt-out flag is set, closing the CLI-side verification as Completed.

**Source ID**: SRC-GDOC-51

# Privacy Design Note: Telemetry Opt-Out Flag Semantics

**Owner**: Diana

**Document Key**: DOC-2051

**Last Updated**: 2026-09-06

## Remaining Limitation

The third-party Electron crash reporter (Sentry) has not been audited for whether it independently respects the opt-out environment variable or requires its own disable hook for minidump uploads.

*Note*: CLI-side telemetry opt-out is verified. Full privacy compliance for air-gapped/opt-out users cannot be claimed until the Sentry crash-reporter path is audited separately.

# Telemetry Opt-Out Flag Semantics

**Owner**: Diana

**Document Key**: DOC-2032

**Last Updated**: 2026-09-06 (retrospective, covers 2026-08-20)

Retrospective decision note on the opt-out flag semantics settled 2026-08-20 for CIPH-48 (Telemetry Opt-Out).

## Decision

The CLI accepts an explicit `--no-telemetry` flag. When present, it must suppress every outbound telemetry call for that invocation, including startup pings and error reports — not just usage-metric events.

**Source ID**: SRC-GDOC-32

# Telemetry Opt-Out Flag Semantics

**Owner**: Diana

**Document Key**: DOC-2032

**Last Updated**: 2026-09-06 (retrospective, covers 2026-08-20)

Retrospective decision note on the opt-out flag semantics settled 2026-08-20 for CIPH-48 (Telemetry Opt-Out).

## Why "explicit" matters

The flag was deliberately specified as opt-out rather than opt-in-by-default-off, since the goal was to give privacy-sensitive users a clear, discoverable switch rather than relying on a config file most users would never find.

**Source ID**: SRC-GDOC-32

I'm organizing the compliance and audit items still pinned to v1.0.0 as of late September 2026, focusing on those outside Docker and Windows packaging. For each one, I need to document the current status, the specific defect or risk it represents, and whether it can be resolved through engineering investigation alone. Starting with CIPH-26, which is an active high-priority audit trail logging issue where CLI-generated audit records don't match the defined specification as of the verification run on September 18th.

For CIPH-40, the third-party license audit is reopened and centers on an AGPL PDF parser dependency—Ghostscript was originally AGPLv3, and the replacement is also AGPL. Charlie's been searching for an Apache or MIT alternative since mid-August without success, and the candidates examined so far don't meet the full feature requirements. This one's trickier because while engineering can search the ecosystem, the outcome depends on whether a suitable parser actually exists; it's not purely an internal fix, so success isn't guaranteed by engineering effort alone.

The OCR training data provenance for tessdata_best is a secondary item—Evan's still tracing whether it's genuinely public domain or CC0, which requires upstream evidence rather than code changes. The Sentry Electron telemetry audit is an engineering task: I need to verify whether the crash reporter respects opt-out settings and add a disable hook if it doesn't, which can be resolved in-house. Finally, there's the Argon2id passphrase hardening that was flagged during the AES-256 sign-off back in August as a pre-v1.0 item, though not a blocker for that sign-off itself.

The air-gapped offline sign-off is explicitly preliminary and doesn't cover side-channel analysis or physical security—it's not a compliance certification. There's also that unresolved 45-second remote license-check hang from CIPH-37. The HIPAA pattern verification report doesn't constitute actual HIPAA compliance; it doesn't assess whether we're covering every HIPAA identifier category in production data. And the offline test harness is still manual, not integrated into CI—it only validates network denial, not full offline batch compliance.

So the real question is whether to flag only the hard blockers or include these open compliance items that constrain what we can claim. CIPH-26 audit trail is the strict release gate, but these others are open items that limit our compliance posture even if they're not formally gating the release. The CIPH-21 release gate lists Docker and Windows as gates, though the audit-log gate was explicitly kept red as a blocker from the September meeting.

Now I'll write this up with proper citations and note the evidence cutoff dates—everything's current through September 18th per the CIPH-26 verification.

content.text:
## Answer

Setting aside the two packaging gates (T005 Docker slim-down/CVE and T029/CIPH-39 Windows code-signing), the dataset shows **one hard compliance blocker** plus **five open compliance/audit items** that constrain what can be claimed for v1.0.0 as of 2026-09-22. No source in the dataset is dated later than 2026-09-18, so every status below is the latest recorded position going into 2026-09-22.

---

### A. Hard release blocker

**1. Audit-trail logging — CLI records don't validate against the schema (CIPH-26 / T016)**

- **Status:** Active, High priority, owner Diana (implementation by Bob). Explicitly held open as a release blocker.
- **Defect:** The design requires a SHA-256 hash of each input stream paired with a companion JSON document recording the redaction map, wired into the CLI batch path. Bob defined the schema on 2026-08-15 and wired CLI integration on 2026-09-10, but Diana's verification pass on **2026-09-18** found the CLI-emitted audit records inconsistent with the defined schema. At the 2026-09-15 pre-release audit Diana stated this "undercuts the audit trail as release evidence" and said she would keep the audit-log gate red until schema and records match; Alice confirmed it stays visible as a release blocker. Bob has "another pass queued."
- **Risk if shipped:** The audit trail — the artifact that ties a redacted output back to a specific input — is not usable as release/compliance evidence.
- **Can engineering close it alone?** **Yes.** This is purely internal: reconcile the emitter with the defined companion JSON schema (or vice versa) and re-run verification. Charlie confirmed in the 2026-09-15 meeting that it "isn't a packaging issue — it's schema versus emitted records." No external party, vendor, or procurement is involved.
- **Sources:** SRC-CU-CIPH-26; SRC-MEET-10 (2026-09-15 Pre-Release Audit); SRC-GDOC-11 (DOC-2011).

---

### B. Open compliance/audit items (not formally listed on the CIPH-21 gate list, but each blocks a compliance claim)

**2. Third-party license audit — AGPL still in the shipped dependency set (CIPH-40 / DOC-2041, DOC-2024)**

- **Status:** **Active (Reopened)**, High priority, owner Diana, search led by Charlie. Last recorded activity 2026-08-15; the 2026-08-21 report states no suitable replacement has been confirmed.
- **Defect:** The initial audit flagged `Ghostscript` (AGPLv3), used by the `rasterizer` module for PDF-to-image conversion, as blacklisted because its viral copyleft terms attach to any binary distributed to partner sites. Evan swapped in a replacement parser on 2026-08-11 and it was marked Completed — but on 2026-08-12 Diana found the replacement was **itself AGPL-licensed**, reintroducing the same license category one layer down. The task was reopened. Alice: AGPL "is a dealbreaker for how we distribute this"; client agreements rule out shipping copyleft in the core engine.
- **Risk:** Shipping v1.0.0 would distribute AGPL code under a distribution model that contractually cannot carry it. The 2026-08-21 report carries an explicit warning: do not report license compliance as resolved externally.
- **Can engineering search alone close it?** **No — search is necessary but not sufficient.** Charlie reported on 2026-08-15 that he had "a couple" of Apache/MIT candidates but "neither one covers everything the old library did," and he explicitly declined to force a bad fit. Closing this needs either (a) a candidate that actually meets the rasterization feature requirements plus the rework to adopt it (Charlie noted the rework cost is unknown until candidates are compared), or (b) a licensing/distribution decision above engineering. A pure search can fail to terminate.
- **Sources:** SRC-CU-CIPH-40; SRC-GDOC-41 (DOC-2041); SRC-GDOC-24 (DOC-2024); SRC-SLACK-40; SRC-SLACK-41; SRC-MEET-08.

**3. OCR training-data provenance unverified (`eng.traineddata` / `tessdata_best`)**

- **Status:** Open, separate and lower-priority sub-item of the license audit, pending Evan's provenance trace. No completion recorded.
- **Defect:** Tesseract OCR itself is Apache 2.0, but the `eng.traineddata` model files were sourced from a community repository and their **training-corpus provenance has not been verified as public-domain/CC0**.
- **Risk:** An unverified-provenance model file ships inside the binary; license compliance cannot be certified while it stands. The audit report names this alongside the parser issue in its "do not report as resolved externally" warning.
- **Can engineering search alone close it?** **No.** This is a documentary provenance trace of a third-party community artifact, not a code or dependency search. Either upstream provenance evidence exists and must be obtained, or the model must be replaced with one having a clean, documented corpus.
- **Sources:** SRC-GDOC-41 (DOC-2041).

**4. Sentry/Electron crash-reporter path not audited against telemetry opt-out (DOC-2051)**

- **Status:** Partially closed. The CLI-side item (CIPH-48) is **Completed** — a 2026-08-24 network trace confirmed zero outbound telemetry with the opt-out flag set, and a design-time pending-queue leak (the `TelemetryLogger` writing to a local SQLite queue during opt-out, which would flush the backlog on re-enable) was patched to a no-op backend. The **crash-reporter path remains unaudited** as of the 2026-09-06 note.
- **Defect:** The third-party Electron crash reporter (Sentry) has not been checked for whether it independently respects the opt-out environment variable or requires its own disable hook for minidump uploads.
- **Risk:** An opted-out or air-gapped user could still emit minidumps. The document states plainly that full privacy compliance for air-gapped/opt-out users **cannot be claimed** until this path is audited separately. Note also Charlie's standing concern that crash reports must not carry PII, which is the whole point of the tool.
- **Can engineering close it alone?** **Yes.** This is an in-house audit of a bundled component plus, if needed, wiring a disable hook. No external dependency.
- **Sources:** SRC-GDOC-51 (DOC-2051); SRC-CU-CIPH-48; SRC-SLACK-62; SRC-SLACK-64.

**5. Air-gapped/offline sign-off is preliminary, not a compliance certification (CIPH-37 / DOC-2047, DOC-2046)**

- **Status:** CIPH-37 is **Completed**, but deliberately scoped. Diana: "I'll close this out, but I want to be clear this is a preliminary offline pass — not a compliance certification." Two residual gaps sit underneath it:
  - **45-second licence-check hang:** the HTTP client reaches for a remote licence server at startup before timing out and falling back to the cached local licence. Logged as a known issue, explicitly **not waived** by the sign-off, and not resolved.
  - **Harness not in CI (DOC-2046, Active):** the network-denial harness runs manually, is not wired into CI, and validates network denial only — it does not itself certify the offline batch run.
- **Risk:** The air-gapped claim rests on a one-off manual pass. The sign-off explicitly does not cover side-channel analysis, physical security, or any regulatory attestation.
- **Can engineering close it alone?** **Split.** The 45-second hang and the CI integration are ordinary engineering work and closable in-house. The **compliance certification / regulatory attestation is not** — that requires an external assessor, and no amount of engineering search produces it.
- **Sources:** SRC-GDOC-47 (DOC-2047); SRC-GDOC-46 (DOC-2046); SRC-CU-CIPH-37; SRC-SLACK-33.

**6. HIPAA pattern coverage verified only against a regression baseline, not certified (CIPH-30 / DOC-2034)**

- **Status:** CIPH-30 is **Completed** — the expanded HIPAA regex dictionary was merged 2026-08-08 and regression-checked against the financial-PII baseline, which passed. But the verification report is explicitly bounded.
- **Gap:** The report "is not a HIPAA compliance certification and does not assess coverage completeness against every HIPAA identifier category in production data." Charlie had flagged during enumeration that many HIPAA identifiers are noisier than the financial patterns.
- **Risk:** Detection coverage across the 18 HIPAA identifier categories is unmeasured against real production data; a coverage claim made on this evidence would overstate what was tested.
- **Can engineering close it alone?** **Partly.** Engineering can build a production-representative coverage assessment; it cannot self-issue a HIPAA certification. Note also that DOC-2047 records no patient records or clinical data were used in testing, so a production-data coverage assessment would additionally need a compliant data source.
- **Sources:** SRC-GDOC-34 (DOC-2034); SRC-CU-CIPH-30; SRC-SLACK-18.

---

### Also noted (adjacent, flagged pre-v1.0)

**Argon2id key-derivation hardening.** At the 2026-08-07 AES-256 at-rest sign-off, Diana signed the pipeline off as Completed but flagged that on machines without a hardware TPM the volume key is still derived from a user passphrase via PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 at 100k iterations. Moving to Argon2id would meaningfully raise the cost of offline brute-force against weak passphrases. This is tracked as a **pre-v1.0 hardening item, explicitly not a sign-off condition** — so it is not blocking, but it is an open pre-v1.0 security item and is fully closable by engineering alone. (SRC-GDOC-35 / DOC-2035.)

---

### Summary table

| # | Item | Status | Engineering alone can close? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Audit-trail CLI/schema mismatch (CIPH-26) | Active — **hard blocker** | **Yes** |
| 2 | AGPL PDF parser in dependency set (CIPH-40) | Active (Reopened) | **No** — search may not terminate; needs feature-viable candidate + rework, or a licensing decision |
| 3 | OCR `eng.traineddata` provenance | Open, lower priority | **No** — documentary provenance / replacement |
| 4 | Sentry crash-reporter vs. opt-out | Unaudited | **Yes** |
| 5 | Air-gapped sign-off preliminary (45s hang; harness not in CI; no attestation) | Task Completed, gaps open | **Partly** — hang + CI yes; certification no |
| 6 | HIPAA coverage not certified / not assessed on production data | Task Completed, gap open | **Partly** — assessment yes; certification no |
| — | Argon2id KDF hardening | Pre-v1.0 item, non-blocking | **Yes** |

**Bottom line:** exactly one compliance item is a formal release blocker beyond packaging — the audit-trail schema mismatch — and it is fully within engineering's control. The item most likely to slip the date is the AGPL parser replacement, because it depends on an ecosystem candidate that did not exist as of the last recorded search. Three further items (OCR provenance, offline compliance certification, HIPAA certification) cannot be closed by engineering search at all; they require external evidence or an external assessor.
